human_tolerance.notes: Occupies 'urban parks, willow thickets, and suburban areas', and 'sunflower seeds are readily taken from bird feeders', which it carries off to a branch to hammer open. The population is thought to be increasing.

phases.name: breeding
phases.note: Nesting season runs from late April through June, with higher-ranking females nesting before lower-ranking ones; breeding pairs form from late fall into winter and the winter flocks disperse into their constituent pairs in spring.

phases.name: nesting
phases.note: A cavity nest 1-7 m above ground, excavated by both sexes or taken from a natural cavity, an old woodpecker nest or a nest box; the female builds it of coarse moss or bark strips lined with fine mammal hair. Usually six to eight eggs, incubated by the female alone for 11-14 days while the male feeds her; young leave the nest 12-16 days after hatching.

phases.name: moult
phases.note: Postnuptial moult at the end of the first summer is partial, covering only body feathers and wing coverts; in later years it is complete. Moultting birds stay silent and hidden.

phases.name: caching
phases.note: Caches mostly seeds, sometimes insects, singly in bark, dead leaves, clusters of conifer needles or knotholes; memory of a cache lasts up to 28 days and the hippocampus is at its largest in October.

phases.name: flocking
phases.note: Forms winter flocks in which strict dominance hierarchies are observable; the flocks include other bird species, and higher-ranking birds get better access to food, hold larger territories and breed more successfully.

vocalizations.description: The two-note 'fee-bee', a simple clear whistle of two notes in identical rhythm, the first roughly a whole step above the second. Sung mainly by males and mainly in relative isolation from other chickadees; both sexes give a faint version when feeding young, the male uses it in courtship, and both sexes use it to call a partner who is out of sight. Young birds in late summer sing a single note.

The familiar 'chick-a-dee-dee-dee' that gave the bird its name, made up of up to four units - A, B and C variations of 'chick-a' and D the repeated 'dee' - and produced by both sexes all year. The number of 'dee' notes rises with the urgency of the message, from contact calls in dense vegetation to recruitment of the flock against a predator.
An explosive hiss like a snake's, given by an incubating female when something unusual disturbs her at the nest entrance; probably an adaptation that discourages nest predators.

external.note: eBird code bcchi via Wikipedia's infobox.

conservation.note: Wikidata P141 = least concern (Q211005); Wikipedia's infobox also carries IUCN3.1 LC.

range.note: Western Alaska through southern Yukon and all the Canadian provinces, and into the United States to northern California, northern Nevada and New Mexico in the southwest and New Jersey in the east, plus the Appalachian Mountains at higher elevations. Elevation band from 'most common at elevations below 750 m ... although they have been known to occur at up to 3,200 m'.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: 'The birds hop along tree branches searching for food, sometimes hanging upside down or hovering; they may make short flights to catch insects in the air.'

traits.nest_type.note: The pair excavates the hole together, uses a natural cavity, reuses an old woodpecker nest, or uses a nest box; two cases of reusing an open cup nest of another species are noted.

traits.perching.note: Hops along branches, hangs upside down and perches to hammer seeds open.

traits.senses.note: The article describes 16 distinct vocalizations and notes that flock members are often out of each other's visual range, which supports High hearing. vision_colour, olfaction, uv and vibration are omitted rather than guessed.

traits.mass_kg.note: Midpoint of Wikipedia's 10-14 g for both sexes.

traits.length_m.note: Derived, not quoted: the article gives no total length, so it is computed from its own standard measurements for a male - mid wing 65.5 mm plus mid tail 60.5 mm is 126 mm, less about 15 mm for the part of the tail base covered by the folded wing tertials, giving roughly 111 mm. The same computation on the female measurements gives about 108 mm. An openly licensed source quoting a total length would have been preferred; none was found.

traits.wingspan_m.note: The weakest number in this record, and flagged as such: the schema requires a wingspan for a flying bird and the article quotes none, only a folded wing chord. Derived as 2.1 times the mid male wing chord of 65.5 mm, the conventional approximation for small passerines with rounded wings, giving about 138 mm. A quoted measurement would replace this.

traits.lifespan_y.note: 'Maximum recorded lifespan is 12 years, although most live roughly 2.5 years.'

traits.diet.note: 'Insects (especially caterpillars) form a large part of their diet in summer. ... Seeds and berries become more important in winter', which the record splits as invertebrate 0.6, seed 0.3 and fruit 0.1. The fat it takes off dead mammals is a trace and is recorded under habitat.resources as a Scavenging use instead of distorting the diet fractions.

traits.social.note: 'This species is a social bird and forms strict dominance hierarchies within its flock', with winter flocks that include other bird species. group_size is authored judgement: the article describes the hierarchy but never states a flock size.

traits.activity_pattern.note: Diurnal: it forages by day in dense vegetation and roosts in cavities and foliage at night.

traits.defense.note: Mob is chosen because the chick-a-dee-dee call is used to recruit the flock against predators; the incubating female's snake-like hiss at a disturbed nest entrance is the second defensive behaviour, recorded as its own call below.

traits.wariness.note: Judgement: 0.25. One of the tamest garden birds in North America - it takes sunflower seeds readily at feeders and occupies suburban areas and urban parks - but it keeps a distance when a person approaches a cavity nest.

habitat.use.note: The arboreal share follows 'the birds hop along tree branches searching for food, sometimes hanging upside down'; the ground share covers coming down to feeders and to hammer seeds on a branch. No open source splits the time, so this is judgement.

habitat.resources.note: Food weights follow traits.diet, plus the carrion entry for the fat off dead mammals. Nesting weight is entirely on cavity; perch and leaf_litter are shelter, weighted by judgement, since leaf litter is named as a cache site rather than a roost.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: 'Urban parks, willow thickets, and suburban areas' are named habitats, sunflower seeds 'are readily taken from bird feeders', and 'the population of black-capped chickadees is thought to be increasing'. impervious_max, flight_distance_m and road_mortality are authored judgement and are not quantified in the source.

habitat.density_per_ha.note: Judgement: no open source gives a density. Small woodland and suburban territories of roughly half a hectare give typical 2 per hectare, and min and max are an authored tenfold band either side, following the convention used for turdus-migratorius and cardinalis-cardinalis.

seasonal.strategy.note: 'Black-capped chickadees are non-migratory', and they do not change habitat between breeding and non-breeding seasons; winter dispersal is described as irregular rather than migratory.

seasonal.phases.note: Late April to June nesting season, cavity height, nest construction by the female only, six to eight eggs, female-only incubation of 11-14 days with the male feeding her, fledging at 12-16 days, the partial first-year and complete postnuptial moult, the single-item seed cache and 28-day cache memory with the October hippocampus peak, and winter flocks with dominance hierarchies are all stated in the article.

seasonal.life_stages.note: Juvenile duration is authored: young leave the nest 12-16 days after hatching and are 'capable of catching food on their own within a week after leaving the nest', which is about three weeks, rounded to 30. First breeding is at one year of age. scale is authored judgement for a small bird.

vocalizations.note: The two-note fee-bee description, its pitch relationship between the notes, the frequency figures (starting around 400 Hz with tones spanning roughly 1 kHz, recorded here as 400-1400 Hz), the four A-D units of the chick-a-dee-dee, its year-round use by both sexes, the faint version used at the nest and in courtship, the single note of young birds in late summer and the incubating female's snake-like hiss are all from the Vocalization and Breeding sections. The chick-a-dee's 3-8 kHz band is authored: the article gives frequency figures for the song only, and places the call's two components on either side of the song, so the band is set around them and is not a quoted measurement. Cooldowns are authored judgement.

look.note: Colours from the Description: a black cap and bib, white cheeks, white underparts with buff-coloured flanks, an unstreaked greenish-grey back, slate-grey wings and tail, a black beak and legs, and dark brown irises. The cap, bib and flank parts render the black cap, black bib and buff flanks that distinguish the bird; the head itself is coloured from the belly slot so the white cheeks read correctly. Proportions are authored judgement for a very small, plump, big-headed bird with short rounded wings. The cap and bib are the only parts kept: light stripes over the eyes, buff flanks and cheek pouches were tried as well and, on a model whose head is 0.95 of torso height, the small boxes overlapped into an unreadable cluster in the previewer.

behavior.note: Authored parameters for the shared perching-songbird program. alarm points at the chick-a-dee-dee call rather than the hiss, since the call is what the flock uses against a threat; food_tag is invertebrate because caterpillars dominate the summer diet the program forages on; flee_m is 5 m for a bold feeder bird; nest_m1 and nest_m2 follow the program's declared params and the 1-7 m cavity height the source gives.
